claims.explanation: This choice does not maximize the product. It gives \((a-b)(c-d)=(10-1)(9-2)=9\cdot 7=63\), but the distinct choice \(a=10,b=2,c=9,d=1\) gives \(8\cdot 8=64\). The two differences cannot both be made as large as possible independently because all four integers must be distinct.

claims.quoted_text: Similarly, if we choose any other combination of \(a, b, c,\) and \(d\) such that the differences \(a - b\) and \(c - d\) are less than 9, the product will be less than 64.
claims.explanation: This is false. Differences 8 and 8 are both less than 9 and give product \(8\cdot 8=64\), exactly as in the preceding example. So the product can equal 64 even when both differences are less than 9.
